After several rounds of discussions between the healthcare management program director (Sean Edmund Rogers) and URI Online leadership, as well as analysis of current and prospective student data, we wish to make the following changes to streamline URI’s healthcare management offerings and to enhance their marketability: 1. Ask #1: Offer a single healthcare management graduate certificate instead of the two separate certificates that currently exist, and allow a wider selection of healthcare management (MHM) courses to count towards that single certificate.

2.
Ask #2: Change the composition of the M.S. degree such that it straightforwardly requires the completion of 30 credits of MHM credits.
Currently, the M.S. degree is structured as the combination of (1) one 12-credit post-baccalaureate certificate, (2) a second post-bac certificate, (3) one MHM elective, and (4) a practicum capstone.
This totals 10 MHM classes and 30 MHM credits.
The certificate portion of this is a so-called stackable certificate approach, with 24 of the 30 credits coming from these two post-bac certificates.
Our desire is to streamline the M.S. in Healthcare Management degree such that it is comprised of 30 MHM credits whether or not a student completes a graduate certificate en passant.
Our primary objective with this entire change proposal is #1 above – to make earning a graduate certificate in healthcare management at URI more accessible.
Per URI Online recruiters and prospectors, there has not been a single expression of interest in the post- bac certificate in quality improvement.

Students are certainly interested in quality improvement and this is an important topic in healthcare; however, none have expressed a desire to devote an entire program of study to this subject.
Any interest in earning a healthcare grad certificate at URI has been directed toward the other existing certificate in health administration.
Additionally, prospective students have expressed strong interest in being able to earn a certificate by taking courses outside of the strict structure that currently exists (at present, three of the four courses in each certificate are prescribed).
The current structure limits when students can begin and complete a certificate – they must wait until the carousel of courses comes back around for them to hop on, and in some cases that can be a year-long wait.
Creating a single certificate in healthcare management enables URI to alleviate these pain points and reach a wider audience of prospective students.
We have found that most prospective students interested in a grad certificate wish to begin quickly, and URI Online has the structure in place to enable that to happen.
The limiting factor is our current program design.

A side effect of creating a single graduate certificate in healthcare management is that the “stackable certificate” design of the M.S. would need to go away and be replaced with a straightforward 30-credit MHM approach.
There is no evidence that removing the notion of stackable certificates would do harm.
No prospects in recent memory have expressed interest in earning the stackable certificates as a pathway to the M.S. degree.
In fact, it has created confusion during prospect calls and sessions. 2

As a final sidenote on the topic of stackable certificates, in my professional opinion (as a scholar of human resources) such a design may even adversely impact URI’s ability to provide accessible healthcare management graduate education to Rhode Islanders and beyond.
As I learned this summer via meetings with enrollment services, financial aid, and URI Online, our healthcare management graduate certificates do not qualify for federal financial aid.
Some graduate certificate programs around the country do qualify for federal aid, but our healthcare management ones were determined not to.
Thus, students must pay for all certificate credits (up to 24 under the current “stackable” model) with non- federal financial aid, such as out of pocket or via private loans.
At current rates, that amounts to $18,792 for two URI certificates.
This has led to more than one prospective student not applying or enrolling at URI this summer and fall.
The streamlining we propose potentially removes barriers to access and may help put URI graduate education within reach for more aspiring healthcare professionals and leaders.

Summary: In sum, the newly-proposed M.S. degree structure would include all the same courses as before.
We are not changing the curricular offering at all - we are simply proposing that the stackable certificate design be removed.
That’s ask #2 above.
And we are asking for it to be removed because we wish to offer a single grad certificate in healthcare management that offers flexibility and frequency for learners (instead of two separate certificates that are narrowly tailored).
That’s ask #1 above. 6.

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) We propose an undergraduate interdisciplinary minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities.
The United Nations defines social justice in terms of human rights and personal dignity for everyone.
Other sources include access and equality.
Borrowing from these descriptions, we define social justice broadly as the value of human life, equal access to social capital, personal dignity, and the implementation of human rights for ALL.
US Citizenship and Immigration Services identifies core civic responsibilities that include staying informed about issues affecting your community and participating in them.
More importantly they add respecting the rights, beliefs, and opinions of others, and participating in the democratic process.
We adopt these descriptions of civic responsibilities for the minor.
Course options for the minor represent an array of multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches to social justice topics.
Students who complete the
3 minor will emerge with a nuanced understanding of the world around them, the

4 reasons why people continue to seek to change that world, and a familiarity with the organizing tools and strategies available to those efforts.
A core intellectual component of the minor is an emphasis on seeing the world through the lens of other people's experiences, especially people and groups who have different social, racial, ethnic, economic, religious, gendered, and geographic backgrounds from one's own.
Developing a critical consciousness of the intersections of one's identities, privileges, and power is another important component.
This can lead to more compassionate and meaningful relationships with others.
Moreover, a deep understanding of one's positionality can help perpetuate or dismantle systems and structures that ultimately impact minoritized communities.
Students will learn about subtle and blatant institutional barriers and the micro-aggressions that systematically oppress people.
Students will have experiential learning opportunities that allow them to see the ways in which the ideas they read about and discuss in class actually play out in the real world.

Students will engage in civic processes visiting with community leaders, activists, and politicians to influence policies.
They will prepare for and engage in civic processes reflecting on these experiences.
They will learn theories, methods, and skills that they can use in their work and personal lives to improve the human condition.
Courses for the minor are organized into three categories; peoples, social and institutional contexts, and methods and skills, and students are required to take at least one course from each category (and not more than three) and then complete their credit requirements in consultation with advisors.
An ongoing advisory committee of faculty, staff, and peers will meet once per semester to review advising strategies, and tweak the course offerings, making sure that courses are still being offered, that faculty who teach them are informed about the minor, and review new course options that become available to include in the minor.
The committee will also develop and distribute marketing materials for the minor and maintain a Google work site for students who pursue the minor and for faculty and staff who contribute to it.

This site will also serve to inform the community about experiential learning opportunities that arise in the interest of social justice and civic responsibilities.
Currently, the committee includes several faculty, staff, and undergraduate students.

Why is the new program being developed?
The world is experiencing monumental institutional changes that have arisen from centuries of oppression against groups of people by age, gender, socioeconomic status, ability, sexual orientation, regionalism, religion, race, ethnicity and nationality.
As a species, we cannot tolerate or participate in group oppression any longer, but the institutionalized nature of systemic oppression requires that people must enter the work- force, build their families, and engage in their communities with the knowledge and skills necessary for creating change.
This is the responsibility of our educational system.

Regardless of a student's major course of study, every one of them should graduate being prepared to create positive change that improves the lives of everyone.
A minor in social justice and civic responsibilities, coupled with the student's major course of study provides a path toward creating positive change in the world.
B2.
What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?
Students who complete the minor will explore their connections to the communities in which they live and work, tackling questions of mutual obligation, social and political change, and human impact on the social, historic, and geographic world.
Grounded in an interdisciplinary approach that includes the humanities, social sciences, the arts, and other fields - this new minor will provide students at URI with a foundation for a life of actively challenging systems of oppression. and decolonizing received wisdom, produced knowledge, and told histories [or public memory].
At the same time, students will gain the critical thinking, reading, writing, and analytical tools that are the foundation of an informed and educated citizenry.

Our students will enter the workforce with skills in human relations that every industry needs for a diverse world.
It is no longer sufficient to train a select few individuals to expertly advise organizations how to navigate diversity.
Everyone must learn the values of a diverse workforce to ensure that each individual can reach their/her/his best potential.
Regardless of a student's major academic and career interests, pursuing the minor in social justice and civic responsibilities will enrich their lives and bring these ideas and skills into all industries, organizations, and occupations.

Since this is a minor and not a major course of study, it is intended to enrich the work and personal lives of everyone, not just those who are in a select few careers.
For example, a student majoring in criminology and criminal justice who pursues a career in policing would be more marketable in that career with a sub-specialty in social justice and civic responsibility, as would a nurse, a teacher, an engineer, or a psychologist, for example.
The skills and information learned in this minor are important for journalists, museum curators, researchers, professors, executive directors of non-profit and social justice organizations, politicians, diplomats, UN officials and advisors, community organizers, community educators (like people at Save the Bay, etc.), entrepreneurs including people piecing together careers through podcasting, and freelance writing.

According to the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training (RIDLT), the top 10 occupations requiring a Bachelor's degree include registered nurses, elementary and secondary school teachers, and child, family & school social workers.
All of these occupations are projected to show increases in job openings through 2026, all of them require extensive work with the public, so this minor would make our graduates more marketable in these careers.
Organizational rules are changing to include more diverse and equitable processes and roles are being introduced to ensure these processes are followed.
Most people who currently occupy positions of power, in this particular moment, were not taught the skills that are necessary to achieve these goals.
They will be looking for people who have received the kind of education that specifically leads to social justice in any occupation.
